body:
OBSERVED on two physical Kobo readers: after a reader was mounted over USB, copied from read-only, cleanly ejected, and then synced over Wi-Fi, Nickel changed locally held books from downloaded to not downloaded. The server acknowledgment later restamped exact same-device entitlement fingerprints and old deletion tombstones even though the underlying book change bases were unchanged.

OBSERVED in cps/kobo.py and the real sync-handler regression: replay suppression and fingerprint loading required SyncToken.is_cwng_token. A partial legacy-shaped token can preserve books_last_modified, selecting only a bounded recent subset, while an omitted archive_last_modified degrades to datetime.min. Because the parser requires all five original cursor fields before setting is_cwng_token, that shape both replays every old tombstone and disables suppression of exact live fingerprints. Empty, malformed, and official-store tokens reset the book cursor too, so they do not explain a bounded recent subset.

OBSERVED fix: exact acknowledged fingerprints are now scoped only by physical device and payload/change basis, not token provenance. Missing device-ledger rows remain recovery work and emit New even behind an advanced cursor. Full Sync and per-book resend deliberately clear target ledger rows, so those explicit recovery actions still redeliver. Deleted-entitlement fingerprints use the same same-device rule.

OBSERVED regression: a partial token selecting 23 recent ledger-backed books while excluding an older row, with five selected books designated as the held subset and three old tombstones, emits 0 NewEntitlement, 0 ChangedEntitlement, and 0 IsRemoved and leaves ledger timestamps untouched. Tokenless exact replay is likewise silent; a missing row and a newly paired reader still receive NewEntitlement; Full Sync restores NewEntitlement.

ASSUMED: the uncaptured post-USB header had this partial JSON shape (book cursors present, archive cursor absent), because it is the only parser-supported shape matching the simultaneous bounded book selection, archive reset, and old suppression refusal. The raw header was not captured, so its exact bytes and which additional fields were present remain unknown.

OBSERVED on hardware against the deployed fixed build, and this closes the finding's one remaining ASSUMED clause. A full mass-storage session was driven end to end from the shell (the reader's own plug-event path, then a clean host-side eject). The reader's automatic sync followed roughly thirty seconds after the eject with no operator or tooling action, and its outgoing token is where the partial shape is produced: it received a populated archive cursor and emitted `archive_modified` = `0001-01-01T00:00:00`. The next sync presented that degraded cursor back, with the book cursors still populated — exactly the shape this finding could previously only infer. The uncaptured post-USB header shape is therefore no longer an inference; it is measured.

OBSERVED on that following request, the fix behaved as designed: `new=0 changed=0 removed=0` with five exact same-reader replays suppressed, `fingerprint_mismatch_reemitted=0`, `reemit_reasons=none`. Read-only device snapshots taken before the session and after the sync are identical: 7 downloaded titles and 231 not downloaded on both sides, with a byte-identical downloaded ContentID set. The per-device entitlement ledger was unchanged across the cycle (242 rows, same digest). Under the pre-fix handler this is precisely the request that re-emitted the held subset as NewEntitlement and made the reader discard the local copies.

CORRECTION to an earlier version of this paragraph, which said the sync carrying the partial token was itself the reader's automatic post-eject sync, about a hundred seconds after the eject. It was not: that particular request was triggered by a deliberate sync action, and a manual and an automatic sync are indistinguishable in the server record. The genuinely automatic post-eject sync is the earlier one, and its role is more specific than the original wording allowed — it does not carry the partial token, it *creates* it, by emitting an archive cursor older than the one it was given.

OBSERVED, and this is the upstream cause rather than a property of the reader: the outgoing archive cursor regresses on a fixed alternating cycle. Across twenty-eight consecutive sync summaries from one day on a live instance, the outgoing archive cursor alternated between a real timestamp and epoch without a single exception — fourteen of twenty-eight emitted `0001-01-01T00:00:00`. The account had no archived books and five deletion tombstones. So the partial token is not something the reader invents after a USB session; the server issues it on every other sync and then declines to trust it on the next one. This finding's fix makes the handler correctly tolerant of that token, which is the right defence and is what stops the de-download. Stopping the server from emitting a regressed cursor at all is tracked separately.

ASSUMED: the pre-fix arm is the original forensic reconstruction rather than a fresh A/B. Deliberately not re-measured — reverting a live instance to the broken handler would de-download real books to prove something already pinned by a regression test that fails without the product change.

CLARIFICATION on the hardware evidence quoted above. That measurement was taken on an instance predating the counter-labelling fix, so in the quoted line `suppressed_unchanged` was a copy of `suppressed_replay` and is not an independent figure. The load-bearing values are unaffected: no entitlement of any kind was emitted (new, changed and removed all zero) and five exact same-reader replays were suppressed. A later cycle on an instance carrying both fixes reproduced the same outcome with correctly separated counters.
title: Partial Kobo sync tokens can replay held-book entitlements and clear downloaded state
